tagline: Horse country and an Ohio River loop along the old highway
intro: US 42 runs through the northern Kentucky hills as a two-lane road between Interstate 71 and the Ohio River. Its Oldham County scenic segment extends from Goshen Lane to KY 3223 and received state designation in 1998. The National Scenic Byway Foundation highlights nearby nature preserves, a loop toward the Ohio River and the horses at Hermitage Farm. At Hermitage, owners Laura Lee Brown and Steve Wilson placed nearly seven hundred acres under a conservation easement to keep it in active farmland permanently.

The larger highway once served travel between cities. In the early 1960s, Interstate 71 took over that role, leaving US 42 as a town-to-town surface road. The scenic designation later recognized this Oldham County stretch; KY 524’s Westport loop received its own designation in 2011. At Westport, the loop reaches an older transport center where steamboats once made regular calls.

Begin at Goshen Lane in Goshen, a town known for thoroughbred breeding farms. Hermitage Farm’s main house predates the Civil War, while the surrounding farm continues its thoroughbred operations. Continue along US 42, taking KY 524 for the Westport loop if desired; it rejoins US 42 at its other end. The designated US 42 drive finishes at KY 3223.

moments.title: Goshen
moments.text: Goshen’s name changed before its formal incorporation, linking two very different references. The community began in 1849 as Saltillo, named for the Mexican city near the Battle of Buena Vista. When a post office opened in 1851, it took the name Goshen from the biblical land that American commentators associated with good soil. The state assembly incorporated the town in 1990. Its agricultural life includes thoroughbred breeding, tree farming and producers of honey and other farm goods. US 42 passes through Goshen before continuing across Oldham County toward Trimble County to the northeast.

moments.title: Hermitage Farm Main House
moments.text: Hermitage’s main house predates the Civil War, but its interior combines antique architecture and furniture with contemporary art. The house and adjacent smokehouse are listed in the National Historic Register. Owners Laura Lee Brown and Steve Wilson bought the farm to protect it from suburban development. Nearly seven hundred acres are now under a conservation easement intended to keep the land in active farming permanently. The main house offers tours when it is not occupied by events or guests. Pin oaks surround the house and frame views across the farmland.

moments.title: Westport
moments.text: Westport’s Ohio River docks once handled a steady movement of settlers and goods. Levi Bowyer operated a ferry to Indiana territory as early as 1800, and steamboats later helped the town grow. By 1818 it was a commercial center, with steamboats and showboats making regular stops. The railroad bypassed Westport, river traffic declined, and an 1884 flood destroyed 27 buildings. Historical Marker 909 recounts the town’s story; the KY 524 loop connects it with US 42. Westport briefly became the county seat in 1826; after its economic decline, many residents moved elsewhere.
